6-6.name: Eval Cases in practice
6-6.note: Patient cases like his past evals. They are made for the Eval mock exam (which always uses them); turn this on to also practice them.

bank.q: The therapeutic index (TI) of a drug is computed as...
bank.why: TI = toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%. LD1 ÷ ED99 is the margin of safety. The bad (toxic) number always goes on top.

bank.q: A drug has a TD50 of 6 mg/kg and an ED50 of 2 mg/kg. What is its therapeutic index?
bank.why: TI = TD50 ÷ ED50 = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 (the slide's own example).
bank.hint: Divide the toxic dose by the effective dose.

bank.q: Four drugs treat the same disease. Which one is the SAFEST?
bank.why: A higher therapeutic index means a wider gap between the toxic and the effective dose, so a safer drug.

bank.q: The margin of safety of a drug is computed as...
bank.why: Margin of safety = lethal dose in 1% ÷ effective dose in 99%: it uses the extremes (edges) of the curves instead of the middles.

bank.term: Why use the margin of safety
bank.q: Why can the margin of safety (LD1 ÷ ED99) be more useful than the therapeutic index?
bank.a: It compares the extremes of the two curves, not their medians
d: It compares only the medians of the curves (LD50 and ED50)
It leaves out the lethal dose and looks only at effects
It is measured in humans, while the index comes from animals
bank.why: The TI compares the 50% points; two drugs with the same TI can still differ at the edges. LD1 ÷ ED99 checks the dose that helps almost everyone against the dose that kills the most sensitive few.

bank.q: Drug A has a margin of safety of 1; Drug B has a margin of safety of 0.0002. Which statement is correct?
bank.a: Drug B is much less safe than Drug A
d: Drug B is much safer than Drug A
The margin of safety does not describe safety
bank.why: Slide example: Drug B (0.002 ÷ 10 = 0.0002) kills some patients at a dose far below what helps everyone. The smaller the margin, the less safe.
bank.hint: Same rule as the TI: bigger is safer.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the four types of therapeutic drug toxicity in the lesson?
bank.why: The four are dose-dependent, allergic, idiosyncratic and drug-drug interactions (DAID).

bank.q: Undesirable drug effects that are NOT deleterious are called...
bank.why: Undesirable effects are either nondeleterious (side effects) or deleterious (toxic effects: pharmacological, pathological or genotoxic).

bank.q: Deleterious (toxic) drug effects are classified as...
d: Type I, II, III or IV
bank.why: Toxic effects = pharmacological (e.g. barbiturate CNS depression), pathological (acetaminophen liver necrosis) or genotoxic (DNA injury).
bank.hint: Drug action, tissue damage, DNA damage.

bank.term: Cancer after years of a drug
bank.q: Darryl develops cancer after taking a drug for 10 years. What type of toxicity is this?
bank.why: Genotoxic effects injure DNA and can be mutagenic or carcinogenic (radiation, environmental chemicals, chemotherapy). This was a midterm item.

bank.q: A patient becomes more and more sedated, then stops breathing, as the dose of phenobarbital is raised. This is an example of...
bank.why: CNS depression by barbiturates is pharmacological toxicity: an exaggerated, dose-dependent version of the drug's own action.
bank.hint: Too much of the drug's normal effect.

bank.q: Hepatocyte necrosis after an acetaminophen overdose is an example of...
bank.why: Pathological toxicity = tissue damage: CYP2E1 makes NAPQI, which kills liver cells once glutathione runs out.

bank.q: A patient gets a severe sunburn-like rash after a short time outdoors while on a drug. Which drug is the lesson's example?
bank.why: Phototoxicity from tetracyclines is listed under pharmacological toxicity. Phenobarbital = barbiturate (CNS depression), primaquine = antimalarial (idiosyncratic hemolysis), acetaminophen = pathological liver injury.

bank.q: Which toxic effect depends mainly on the DURATION of drug exposure?
d: Anaphylaxis from a type I reaction
bank.why: Slides: barbiturate CNS depression is dose-dependent, tardive dyskinesia depends on duration (it appears after months to years).

bank.q: Which extrapyramidal symptom appears LAST after an antipsychotic is started?
bank.why: Order of onset: acute dystonia (hours–5 days) → parkinsonism (5–30 days) → akathisia (5–60 days) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years). D-P-A-T.

bank.q: A day after starting an antipsychotic, a teenager suddenly has a twisted neck and a protruding, spasming tongue. This is...
bank.why: Acute dystonia comes first (hours to 5 days): spasms of the tongue, neck, face and back.

bank.q: Two weeks into antipsychotic treatment, Marco has a tremor, a shuffling gait, drooling and a stooped posture. This is...
bank.why: Parkinsonism appears at 5–30 days with tremor, shuffling gait, drooling and stooped posture.

bank.q: After three weeks on an antipsychotic, Cas cannot sit still; she keeps getting up and pacing the room. This is...
bank.why: Akathisia (5–60 days) = compulsive, repetitive motion and restlessness.

bank.q: After years of antipsychotic use, a patient keeps smacking his lips and darting his tongue in and out ("fly-catching"). This is...
bank.why: Tardive dyskinesia appears after months to years: lip-smacking, worm-like tongue movements, fly-catching tongue.

bank.q: Which is NOT listed in the lesson as a cause of genotoxic effects?
bank.why: Genotoxic causes: ionizing radiation, environmental chemicals and chemotherapy, which injure DNA. Barbiturates are the example of pharmacological (CNS depression) toxicity.
bank.hint: Which one causes sedation, not DNA damage?

bank.q: The incidence and seriousness of dose-dependent toxicity are proportional to the drug's concentration in the body and the duration of exposure.
bank.why: Both the concentration and the duration of exposure matter for dose-dependent reactions.

bank.q: A drug with a higher therapeutic index is less safe.
bank.why: The opposite: a higher TI means the toxic dose is far above the effective dose, so the drug is safer.

bank.q: Which type of hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE on mast cells and basophils, with histamine release?
bank.why: Type I = anaphylactic: IgE + histamine → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, capillary leak, swelling. ACID: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed.

bank.q: The Arthus reaction is which type of hypersensitivity?
bank.why: Type III = Arthus reaction (immune complex). ACID: the third letter is Immune complex.

bank.q: A cytolytic (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction is...
bank.why: Type II = cytolytic (cytotoxic). ACID: the C is second.

bank.q: A T-cell–mediated hypersensitivity that appears a day or more after exposure is...
bank.why: Type IV = delayed, cell-mediated (T cells); no antibodies involved.
bank.hint: D for delayed, the last letter of ACID.

bank.q: Which antibody crosses the placenta?
bank.why: IgG is the main antibody in blood and the only one that crosses the placenta. IgE = allergy, IgM = first responder, IgA = secretions.
bank.hint: The most common antibody in blood.

bank.q: Which antibody binds mast cells and basophils in allergic reactions?
bank.why: IgE drives allergy (type I) and fights parasites by binding mast cells and basophils.

bank.q: Which antibody is found in saliva, tears and colostrum?
bank.why: IgA protects mucosal surfaces and is in secretions, including breast milk (colostrum).
bank.hint: A for the antibody in secretions.

bank.q: Which antibody is the first responder and fixes complement?
bank.why: IgM appears first in an immune response and activates complement. IgD is the B-cell receptor.

bank.q: An abnormal reactivity to a chemical that is peculiar to a given individual is called...
bank.why: Idiosyncrasy is a peculiar, usually genetic, reaction in one person. Example on the slide: primaquine hemolysis.

bank.q: A drug causes hemolytic anemia in about 10% of black males, the lesson's example of an idiosyncratic reaction. Which drug is it?
bank.why: Primaquine (antimalarial) → hemolytic anemia in ~10% of black males: an idiosyncratic (genetic) reaction. Tetracycline = phototoxicity, acetaminophen = liver necrosis, phenobarbital = CNS depression.

bank.q: What are the five levels of drug-drug interaction, in order?
bank.a: Absorption, protein binding, metabolism, receptor binding, therapeutic action
d: Metabolism, absorption, receptor binding, protein binding, therapeutic action
Protein binding, absorption, therapeutic action, metabolism, receptor binding
Absorption, metabolism, protein binding, therapeutic action, receptor binding
bank.why: Follow the drug's journey: absorbed → rides on proteins → metabolized → hits a receptor → makes an effect.

bank.q: Ranitidine taken with triazolam increases the amount of triazolam absorbed. At what level is this interaction?
bank.why: Ranitidine (H2 blocker) raises GI pH, which may increase the absorption of basic drugs such as triazolam.

bank.q: How does ranitidine increase the absorption of triazolam?
bank.why: Ranitidine is an H2 antagonist; less stomach acid means a higher pH, so more of a basic drug stays un-ionized and is absorbed.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT among the highly protein-bound drugs listed in the lesson?
bank.why: Highly bound: aspirin, barbiturates, phenytoin, sulfonamides, valproic acid, warfarin. Ranitidine is the absorption example.
bank.hint: Which one is the gut-pH example?

bank.q: Warfarin is highly bound to albumin. A second drug with a higher affinity for albumin is added. What happens to warfarin?
d: Nothing; bound warfarin is the active form
bank.why: The new drug displaces warfarin from albumin, so more warfarin is free and active (risk of bleeding). Only free drug acts.

bank.q: Which substance is a potent inducer of CYP2E1?
bank.why: Metabolic interactions usually involve hepatic CYPs; ethanol is a potent CYP2E1 inducer (which is why drinkers make more NAPQI from acetaminophen).

bank.q: Mr. Lim, in treatment for opioid addiction, no longer feels euphoria when he secretly uses another narcotic. Which drug is he most likely taking?
bank.why: Buprenorphine is an opioid partial agonist/antagonist: it treats opioid addiction and blocks the euphoria of other narcotics (a receptor-binding interaction). Flumazenil = benzodiazepine antidote.

bank.q: Buprenorphine blocking the euphoria of other narcotics is an interaction at the level of...
bank.why: Both drugs compete at the opioid receptor; buprenorphine's partial agonism blunts the other narcotic.

bank.q: Two drugs given together produce an effect greater than the sum of their separate effects (1 + 1 > 2). This is...
bank.why: Additive = 1 + 1 = 2; synergistic = 1 + 1 > 2; antagonistic = 1 + 1 < 2.

bank.q: Two drugs given together produce exactly the sum of their separate effects (1 + 1 = 2). This is...
bank.why: Additive: the effects simply add up.

bank.q: EDTA binds lead into a water-soluble complex that is excreted. Which kind of antagonism is this?
bank.why: Chemical antagonism: one drug binds and inactivates the other (chelators like EDTA).

bank.q: Two drugs act on DIFFERENT receptors and produce opposite effects. Which kind of antagonism is this?
bank.why: Functional/physiological antagonism: opposite effects through different receptors. F-C-D-R: Fight from another receptor, Chemically grab it, Dispose of it, block the Receptor.

bank.q: One drug lowers the effect of another by changing its absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion. This is...
bank.why: Dispositional = changes the other drug's ADME (for example a CYP inducer that clears it faster).

bank.q: A competitive receptor antagonist's effect can be overcome by giving more agonist. This is called...
bank.why: Competitive antagonists share the agonist's site, so more agonist wins (surmountable). Noncompetitive antagonism is unsurmountable.

bank.q: A noncompetitive receptor antagonist can be overcome by giving more agonist.
bank.why: Noncompetitive antagonism is unsurmountable; only competitive antagonism is overcome by more agonist.

bank.q: Medication errors are about how many times more common than adverse drug reactions?
bank.why: Slide: medication errors are 50–100× more common than adverse drug reactions.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the "five rights" of safe medication administration?
bank.why: The five rights: right drug, right patient, right dose, right route, right time.

bank.q: Which is a LONG-TERM (technology-based) recommendation to reduce medication errors?
d: Removing concentrated KCl from patient areas
bank.why: Long term = technology: computerized order entry, dose and allergy checking, medication tracking, bar codes. The others are short-term steps.

bank.q: Which is a SHORT-TERM recommendation to reduce medication errors?
bank.a: Removing concentrated KCl from patient care areas
bank.why: Short term: unit-dose systems, pharmacy-prepared IV solutions, removing dangerous drugs like concentrated KCl, special procedures for high-risk drugs, education. Computers and bar codes are long term.

bank.q: A poisoning-prevention strategy that requires NO behavior change from the individual is...
bank.why: Passive strategies work without anyone changing behavior (child-resistant packaging); active ones need sustained adaptation.

bank.q: Putting medicines in child-resistant packaging is which kind of prevention, and how does it work?
bank.a: Passive: it prevents access to the poison
d: Passive: it changes the product's formulation
Active: it reduces the sale of the poison
bank.why: Table 4-6: child-resistant packaging prevents access, a passive strategy.

bank.q: Limiting the number of pills in a single bottle of baby aspirin is an example of...
bank.a: Decreasing the amount of poison in a product
d: Reducing the manufacture or sale of a poison
bank.why: Passive strategies (Table 4-6): reduce manufacture/sale (phenformin withdrawn), decrease the amount (fewer baby aspirin pills), prevent access (child-resistant packaging), change formulation (no ethanol in mouthwash).

bank.q: Withdrawing phenformin from the U.S. market is an example of which passive strategy?
bank.a: Reducing the manufacture or sale of a poison
d: Decreasing the amount of poison in a product
bank.why: Phenformin was withdrawn from the market: reducing manufacture/sale.

bank.q: Removing ethanol from mouthwash is an example of...
d: Reducing the manufacture or sale of a poison
bank.why: Changing what the product contains = changing the formulation (passive).

bank.q: What is the FIRST priority in treating a poisoned patient?
d: Combat the poison at its effector sites
bank.why: Priorities: 1) maintain vital functions, 2) reduce absorption and enhance elimination, 3) combat the toxic effects at the effector sites.

bank.q: In the ABCDE of initial stabilization, what does D (Disability) assess?
bank.why: D = disability: assess CNS dysfunction; if present, consider O2, dextrose, naloxone and thiamine.

bank.q: A poisoned patient has neurological disability. Which is NOT among the treatments to consider?
bank.why: Box 4-3: consider O2 (check pulse oximetry), dextrose (check glucose), naloxone (empiric trial) and thiamine. Atropine is for cholinergic poisoning.

bank.q: During initial stabilization, thiamine is given to adult patients who are receiving...
bank.why: Box 4-3: thiamine for adult patients receiving dextrose.

bank.q: In ABCDE, E (Exposure) means assessing the...
bank.why: E = exposure: look for the toxidrome (the pattern of findings that points to the poison).

bank.q: In ABCDE, B (Breathing) means...
bank.why: A = airway patency, B = oxygenation and ventilation, C = perfusion of vital organs, D = CNS, E = toxidrome.

bank.q: What is the first step in decontaminating a poisoned patient?
bank.why: Decontamination: first stop the ongoing exposure, then wash eyes and skin copiously; GI decontamination only for ingestions that meet the conditions.

bank.q: Gabriel was sprayed with pesticide in the field. His airway and breathing are secured. What should be done next to decontaminate him?
bank.a: Remove his contaminated clothes and wash his skin copiously
d: Give syrup of ipecac to make him vomit
Start whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
Give activated charcoal by mouth or nasogastric tube
bank.why: For skin exposure, stop the ongoing exposure (remove contaminated clothing) and wash the skin and eyes copiously. GI methods are for swallowed poisons.
bank.hint: The poison is on him, not in his gut.

bank.q: Eyes and skin exposed to a poison should be...
d: Neutralized with a strong acid or base
bank.why: Slide: eyes and skin should be washed copiously.

bank.q: GI decontamination is done only if all of these are true EXCEPT...
bank.a: The poison has already been fully absorbed
d: The poison is still unabsorbed in the stomach or intestine
The procedure can be done safely with proper technique
bank.why: All three must hold: dangerous poison, still unabsorbed, and safe to do. If it's already absorbed, GI decontamination can't help.
bank.hint: Nothing left in the gut to remove.

bank.q: Which is NOT a GI decontamination method listed in the lesson?
bank.why: GI methods: activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation, cathartics, gastric lavage, syrup of ipecac. Hemodialysis removes poison from the blood, not the gut.

bank.q: Which GI decontamination method binds the toxicant in the gut?
bank.why: Activated charcoal adsorbs (binds) the poison; ipecac causes vomiting, cathartics and whole-bowel irrigation push it through faster.

bank.q: Adverse drug reactions are more common than medication errors.
bank.why: Medication errors are 50–100 times MORE common than adverse drug reactions.

bank.q: Ms. Torres swallowed a whole bottle of acetaminophen. Which antidote should she get?
bank.why: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) refills glutathione to neutralize NAPQI. Naloxone = opioids, flumazenil = benzodiazepines, fomepizole = methanol/ethylene glycol.

bank.q: A toddler swallowed many of his mother's iron tablets. Which antidote?
bank.why: Deferoxamine chelates iron (de-FE-roxamine). Dimercaprol and EDTA are for lead (and other metals), penicillamine for copper.

bank.q: Which chelator is listed for COPPER poisoning?
bank.why: Penicillamine: lead, mercury, copper (Peni-copper). Deferoxamine = iron; succimer = lead, mercury, arsenic; EDTA = lead.

bank.q: Which antidote is listed for LEAD only (not mercury or arsenic)?
bank.why: EDTA (calcium disodium) = lead. Dimercaprol and succimer = lead, mercury, arsenic; penicillamine = lead, mercury, copper.
bank.hint: The one with calcium in it.

bank.q: Which antidote covers lead, mercury AND arsenic?
bank.why: Dimercaprol (BAL) and succimer (DMSA) both cover lead, mercury and arsenic. Penicillamine covers copper instead of arsenic.

bank.q: After drinking homemade lambanog, a man has blurred vision and severe acidosis from methanol. Which antidote blocks alcohol dehydrogenase?
bank.why: Fomepizole (or ethanol) blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so methanol and ethylene glycol aren't turned into toxic acids. Don't confuse fomepizole with flumazenil (benzodiazepines).

bank.q: Besides fomepizole, which antidote is used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning?
bank.why: Ethanol competes for alcohol dehydrogenase, like fomepizole.

bank.q: A man found unresponsive has pinpoint pupils and very slow breathing after using heroin. Which antidote?
bank.why: Naloxone = opioid antagonist. Flumazenil = benzodiazepines, atropine = organophosphates, glucagon = β-blockers.

bank.q: A patient took too many lorazepam tablets and is deeply sedated. Which antidote?
bank.why: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine (it's also one of the UGT drugs in Lesson 2); flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist.

bank.q: Which pair is the antidote for organophosphate pesticide poisoning?
bank.why: Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects of the excess ACh; pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase. Physostigmine and neostigmine would make it worse (they inhibit AChE).
bank.hint: Block the receptor + regenerate the enzyme.

bank.q: A child is hot, dry, flushed, has dilated pupils and is agitated after an overdose of an anticholinergic drug. Which antidote?
bank.why: Physostigmine is the antidote for anticholinergic syndrome: an AChE inhibitor that enters the brain. Neostigmine doesn't enter the CNS; atropine would worsen it.

bank.q: After a propranolol overdose, a patient has severe bradycardia and hypotension. Which antidote?
bank.why: Glucagon raises heart cAMP without using β-receptors, bypassing the blockade. Propranolol is a nonselective β-blocker (-olol).
bank.hint: It works around the blocked receptor.

bank.q: A woman overdosed on her verapamil. Which antidote is listed for Ca2+ channel blockers?
bank.why: Table 4-9: high-dose insulin and calcium (gluconate or chloride) for Ca2+ channel blockers. Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine CCB (Lesson 6).

bank.q: Which antidote is used for digoxin (cardiac glycoside) toxicity?
bank.why: Digoxin immune Fab = antibody fragments that bind digoxin.

bank.q: A fire victim with soot in the mouth has severe lactic acidosis from cyanide in the smoke. Which antidote?
bank.why: Cyanide: hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate. Methylene blue = methemoglobinemia, deferoxamine = iron, leucovorin = methotrexate.

bank.q: Which antidote treats methemoglobinemia?
bank.why: Methylene blue turns methemoglobin (Fe3+) back into hemoglobin (Fe2+).

bank.q: A family is found drowsy with headaches in a closed room where a generator was running. Which treatment is listed?
bank.why: Carbon monoxide → hyperbaric oxygen, which pushes CO off hemoglobin.

bank.q: A patient on warfarin is bleeding from the gums with a very high INR. Which antidote?
bank.why: Vitamin K1 restores clotting-factor synthesis blocked by coumarins (warfarin) and indandione.

bank.q: Which antidote is used for methotrexate toxicity?
bank.why: Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the folate step methotrexate blocks.

bank.q: Tracy, who takes glipizide, keeps having low blood sugar even after IV dextrose. Which antidote stops the excess insulin release?
bank.why: Octreotide (a somatostatin analog) is the antidote for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia. Glipizide is a 2nd-generation sulfonylurea. This came out in the midterm.

bank.q: A patient on TB treatment who took extra isoniazid tablets is having seizures. Which antidote?
bank.why: Isoniazid depletes vitamin B6; pyridoxine treats isoniazid seizures.

bank.q: Which antidote is used for valproate-induced hyperammonemia?
bank.why: Table 4-9: carnitine for valproate hyperammonemia.

bank.q: Hours after an antipsychotic injection, a patient's neck twists and his eyes roll up. Which antidote is listed for drug-induced dystonia?
bank.why: Drug-induced (acute) dystonia: benztropine or diphenhydramine (anticholinergic). Dantrolene = malignant hyperthermia, bromocriptine = neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

bank.q: Which antidote is listed for neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
bank.why: Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) for NMS, the dangerous antipsychotic reaction.

bank.q: During surgery under general anesthesia, a patient's muscles become rigid and his temperature soars. Which antidote?
bank.why: Dantrolene stops calcium release in skeletal muscle: the antidote for malignant hyperthermia.

bank.q: Which antidote is used for poisoning by Na+ channel-blocking drugs?
bank.why: Table 4-9: sodium bicarbonate for Na+ channel-blocking drugs.

bank.q: Besides Ca2+ channel blockers, calcium gluconate or chloride is the antidote for...
bank.why: Table 4-9: calcium gluconate/chloride for Ca2+ channel-blocking drugs and fluoride.

bank.q: Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab is used for...
bank.why: Crotalidae immune Fab binds rattlesnake (crotaline) venom.

bank.q: Which of these antidotes is a chelator?
bank.why: Chelators grab metals: dimercaprol, succimer, EDTA, penicillamine, deferoxamine.

bank.q: Which antidote works by replenishing glutathione?
bank.why: NAC refills glutathione so NAPQI from acetaminophen is neutralized.

bank.q: Physostigmine is the antidote for anticholinergic syndrome.
bank.why: Physostigmine is an AChE inhibitor that enters the brain, so it reverses central and peripheral anticholinergic toxicity.

bank.q: Flumazenil reverses opioid overdose.
bank.why: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; naloxone reverses opioids.

bank.q: Octreotide is the antidote for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia.
bank.why: Octreotide (somatostatin analog) stops insulin release driven by sulfonylureas.

bank.q: Substances that are foreign to the body, which drug metabolism prepares for elimination, are called...
bank.why: Drug metabolism turns xenobiotics into forms the body can eliminate, using the same enzymes it uses for dietary substances.

bank.q: What is the usual order of drug handling in the liver?
bank.a: Phase I oxidation → Phase II conjugation → Phase III transport
d: Phase II conjugation → Phase I oxidation → Phase III transport
Phase III transport → Phase I oxidation → Phase II conjugation
Phase I conjugation → Phase II oxidation → Phase III transport
bank.why: Phase I (CYP450 oxidation) → Phase II (conjugation) → Phase III (ABC transporters) → excretion in urine or bile.
bank.hint: Change it, attach to it, push it out.

bank.q: Which is NOT a Phase 1 reaction?
bank.why: Phase 1 = oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Glucuronidation is a Phase 2 conjugation (UGTs).
bank.hint: Phase 1 changes the molecule; it doesn't attach a big group.

bank.q: Which is a Phase 2 (conjugation) reaction?
bank.why: Phase 2 attaches a group: glucuronidation, sulfation, glutathione conjugation, acetylation, methylation.

bank.q: Which statement about Phase 1 metabolism is true?
bank.a: It adds or exposes a functional group and only slightly raises water solubility
d: It attaches a large polar group, making the drug very water-soluble
It moves the drug out of the cell with ABC transporters
bank.why: Phase 1 adds a handle (–OH, –COOH, –SH, –O–, NH2): little gain in solubility but a big change in activity, often inactivation. Phase 2 makes it very water-soluble; Phase 3 transports it out.

bank.q: What is the main result of Phase 2 conjugation?
bank.a: A much more water-soluble metabolite that is easier to eliminate
d: A more lipid-soluble metabolite that enters the brain
A slightly modified molecule with a new –OH group
Transport of the drug out of the cell
bank.why: Phase 2 attaches a large polar group ("2gether"), so the metabolite dissolves in water and washes out in urine or bile.

bank.q: Phase III of drug handling involves...
bank.a: Transport out of the cell by ABC transporters
bank.why: Phase III = transport (ABC transporters) into urine or bile.

bank.q: Phenytoin is hydroxylated by a CYP to 4-hydroxyphenytoin, which is then made into a very soluble glucuronide. Which enzyme makes the glucuronide?
bank.why: Slide example: phenytoin → (Phase 1, CYP) → 4-hydroxyphenytoin → (Phase 2, UGT) → glucuronide.
bank.hint: The enzyme that adds glucuronic acid.

bank.q: Cytochrome P450 enzymes are...
bank.why: CYPs = heme bound noncovalently to a polypeptide. FMOs are the flavin-containing ones.
bank.hint: Like the iron center of hemoglobin.

bank.q: About what share of drug metabolism do CYPs handle?
bank.why: CYPs handle about 75% of drug metabolism.

bank.q: In the name CYP3A4, what does the letter A stand for?
bank.why: CYP3A4 = family 3, subfamily A, gene 4.
bank.hint: CYP names go: number, letter, number.

bank.q: Which CYP metabolizes over 50% of drugs?
bank.why: CYP3A4 metabolizes over half of all drugs; families 1, 2 and 3 do drug metabolism (most active: 2C, 2D, 3A).

bank.q: Which CYP families do most drug metabolism?
bank.why: CYP1, CYP2 and CYP3 do drug metabolism; the most active are CYP2C, CYP2D and CYP3A.

bank.q: Which reaction is NOT catalyzed by CYPs?
bank.why: CYP reactions: N- and O-dealkylation, aromatic hydroxylation, N- and S-oxidation, deamination, dehalogenation. Sulfation is Phase 2 (SULTs).

bank.q: Testosterone is converted to estradiol by aromatase. Which statement about aromatase is correct?
bank.a: It is CYP19, a Phase 1 (CYP) enzyme
bank.why: Aromatase = CYP19, a CYP that also makes steroids. A midterm true-or-false said testosterone → estradiol is done by Phase II enzymes: that is FALSE.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits CYP19 (aromatase)?
bank.why: Anastrozole blocks aromatase. Omeprazole and isoniazid are CYP inhibitors in general (SICKFACES.COM); rifampin is an inducer.

bank.q: Which statement about flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs) is true?
bank.a: They form benign products and cause few drug-drug interactions
d: They are the main drug-metabolizing enzymes
bank.why: FMOs are minor Phase 1 contributors with benign products and fewer interactions. The heme ones are the CYPs.

bank.q: Which FMO is the most abundant?
bank.why: Six FMO families; FMO3 is the most abundant.

bank.q: Which drug is metabolized mainly by FMOs?
bank.why: FMO substrates: nicotine, H2 blockers (cimetidine, ranitidine), clozapine, itopride. Acetaminophen and morphine go through UGT; isoniazid through NAT.

bank.q: Which group of drugs is metabolized by FMOs?
bank.why: FMOs: nicotine, cimetidine, ranitidine, clozapine, itopride. The other groups are UGT, NAT and GST drugs.

bank.q: Which is a Phase 1 enzyme other than the CYPs and FMOs?
bank.why: Other Phase 1: epoxide hydrolases, alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, NQO. UGT, NAT and TPMT (a methyltransferase) are Phase 2.

bank.q: Phase 1 metabolism can dramatically change a drug's activity, often inactivating it.
bank.why: Phase 1 changes little in solubility but a lot in activity, usually inactivation (sometimes activation).

bank.q: Testosterone is converted to estradiol by Phase II enzymes.
bank.why: Aromatase (CYP19) is a CYP, a Phase I enzyme. (Midterm item.)

bank.q: A CYP inducer added to a patient's drugs will usually ___ the levels of other drugs metabolized by that CYP.
bank.why: Inducers make more enzyme → faster metabolism → lower levels and less effect of the other drug.

bank.q: A CYP inhibitor added to a patient's drugs will usually...
bank.a: Raise the levels of other drugs, risking toxicity
d: Lower the levels of other drugs, causing loss of effect
Have no effect on other drugs
Speed up the elimination of other drugs
bank.why: Inhibitors slow metabolism, so other drugs build up (toxicity).

bank.q: Aaliya takes a CYP-metabolized drug. She is then diagnosed with diabetes and starts glipizide. Glipizide is a...
bank.why: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea, and sulfonylureas are the last S of the inducer list BULLSHIT CRAP GP'S. This was a midterm item.
bank.hint: What class is glipizide, and which list has that class?

bank.q: Following the case above: glipizide induces the CYP that clears Aaliya's first drug. What should happen to that drug's dose?
d: No change; they are not related
bank.why: An inducer clears the first drug faster, so its level falls; the dose is increased to keep the effect. (Midterm item, linked to the one before.)

bank.q: Princess takes a CYP-metabolized drug and starts rifampin for tuberculosis. What should happen to the first drug's dose?
bank.why: Rifampin is a CYP inducer (the R in CRAP), so the other drug is cleared faster and needs a higher dose.

bank.q: A patient on a CYP-metabolized drug is started on ketoconazole for a fungal infection. What should you watch for?
bank.a: Toxicity from higher levels of the first drug
d: Loss of effect from lower levels
Faster elimination of the first drug
bank.why: Ketoconazole is a CYP inhibitor (the K in SICKFACES.COM), so the other drug accumulates.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INDUCER?
bank.why: Inducers (BULLSHIT CRAP GP'S): barbiturates, St. John's Wort, carbamazepine, rifampin, alcohol (chronic), phenytoin, griseofulvin, phenobarbital, sulfonylureas. The others are inhibitors.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INDUCER?
bank.why: Rifampin is the R in CRAP. Ketoconazole, ciprofloxacin and omeprazole are in SICKFACES.COM (inhibitors).

bank.q: Which is a CYP INDUCER?
bank.why: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4. Grapefruit juice, amiodarone and metronidazole inhibit CYPs.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INDUCER?
bank.why: Phenytoin is the P in CRAP. Sodium valproate is the first S of SICKFACES; fluconazole and chloramphenicol are inhibitors too.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INDUCER?
bank.why: Griseofulvin (antifungal) is the G in GP'S, an inducer, while ketoconazole and fluconazole (also antifungals) are inhibitors. Trap: not every antifungal inhibits.

bank.q: Which of these is in the CYP INDUCER list?
bank.why: Look-alike trap: sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide…) INDUCE; sulfonamides (antibiotics) INHIBIT.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Cimetidine is the first C in SICKFACES.COM. Phenobarbital, rifampin and carbamazepine are inducers.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Ketoconazole = the K in SICKFACES. The others induce.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Erythromycin = the E in SICKFACES. Barbiturates, rifampin and glipizide (a sulfonylurea) induce.

bank.q: Which TB drug is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Isoniazid is the I in SICKFACES; rifampin, the other TB drug, is an inducer.

bank.q: Which drug is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Omeprazole = the O in .COM. The others are inducers.

bank.q: Which antibiotic is a CYP INHIBITOR?
bank.why: Ciprofloxacin = the C in .COM; metronidazole is the M.

bank.q: Mara's drug levels became toxic after she started drinking grapefruit juice every morning. Why?
bank.a: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP metabolism of her drug
d: Grapefruit juice raises the GI pH
Grapefruit juice displaces her drug from albumin
bank.why: Grapefruit juice (with amiodarone and quinidine) is listed with the CYP inhibitors.

bank.q: Which added drug would most likely RAISE the blood level of a CYP3A4-metabolized drug?
bank.why: Fluconazole is a CYP inhibitor (the F in SICKFACES). The others are inducers and would lower the level.

bank.q: Which added drug would most likely LOWER the blood level of a CYP-metabolized drug?
bank.why: Phenobarbital is an inducer (the P in GP'S). The others are inhibitors.

bank.q: Alcohol appears in both the inducer and the inhibitor lists. Which is correct?
bank.a: Chronic drinking induces CYPs; an acute binge inhibits them
d: Chronic drinking inhibits; an acute binge induces
bank.why: Chronic alcohol use induces (BULLSHIT CRAP: A = alcohol, chronic); an acute binge inhibits (SICKFACES: A = alcohol, binge).

bank.q: St. John's Wort clears CYP3A4 substrates faster because it...
bank.why: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4.

bank.q: In SICKFACES.COM (CYP inhibitors), the K stands for...
bank.why: S-I-C-K: sodium valproate, isoniazid, cimetidine, ketoconazole.

bank.q: In BULLSHIT CRAP GP'S (CYP inducers), the R stands for...
bank.why: C-R-A-P: carbamazepine, rifampin, alcohol (chronic), phenytoin.

bank.q: Sulfonamides are CYP inducers.
bank.why: Sulfonamides are CYP INHIBITORS (the S in SICKFACES). Sulfonylureas are the inducers.

bank.q: Cimetidine is a CYP inhibitor.
bank.why: Cimetidine is the first C in SICKFACES.COM.

bank.q: Phase 2 enzymes are also called...
bank.why: Phase 2 enzymes transfer a group onto the drug: UGTs, SULTs, GSTs, NATs, MTs.

bank.q: UGTs transfer glucuronic acid from...
bank.why: UGT uses UDP-GA; SULT uses PAPS; methyltransferases use SAM; NATs use acetyl-CoA.

bank.q: Sulfotransferases (SULTs) get their sulfate from...
bank.why: SULTs transfer sulfate from PAPS.

bank.q: Methyltransferases use which methyl donor?
bank.why: O-, N- and S-methylation all use SAM.

bank.q: Which Phase 2 reaction accounts for the largest share of Phase 2 metabolism?
bank.why: UGTs (glucuronidation) do the largest share of Phase 2.

bank.q: Which drug is cleared mainly by glucuronidation, per the lesson?
bank.why: UGT drugs: acetaminophen, morphine, oxazepam, lorazepam. Isoniazid = NAT, busulfan = GST, mercaptopurine = methylation.

bank.q: Which group of drugs is glucuronidated by UGTs?
bank.why: UGT: acetaminophen, morphine, oxazepam, lorazepam. The other groups are NAT, GST and MT drugs.

bank.q: Defects in UGT1A1, which glucuronidates bilirubin, cause...
bank.why: UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin; defects cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar).

bank.q: Which drug induces UGT1A1?
bank.why: Phenobarbital induces UGT1A1 (and CYPs). The others are CYP inhibitors.

bank.q: Which drug is sulfated by SULTs, per the lesson?
bank.why: SULT drugs: acetaminophen, steroids, methyldopa. Morphine = UGT, isoniazid = NAT, busulfan = GST.

bank.q: In the fetus, adrenal SULT2A1 makes DHEA-S, which is used for...
bank.why: Fetal adrenal SULT2A1 → DHEA-S → placental estrogen in the second half of pregnancy. SULT2B1b makes cholesterol sulfate in the skin.

bank.q: SULT2B1b in the skin makes cholesterol sulfate for...
bank.why: SULT2B1b → cholesterol sulfate → keratinocyte differentiation.

bank.q: Glutathione is a tripeptide of...
bank.why: Glutathione = Glu-Cys-Gly.

bank.q: Which drug is conjugated by glutathione S-transferases (GSTs)?
bank.why: GST drugs: adriamycin, fosfomycin, busulfan.

bank.q: N-acetyltransferases act on drugs that have...
bank.a: An aromatic amine or hydrazine group
bank.why: NATs acetylate aromatic amines and hydrazines (isoniazid is a hydrazine).

bank.q: Which drug is metabolized by N-acetylation?
bank.why: NAT drugs: sulfonamides, isoniazid, dapsone, clonazepam (also hydralazine, procainamide).

bank.q: Josef, a slow acetylator, develops numbness and tingling of his feet and abnormal liver tests during TB treatment. Which drug is responsible?
bank.why: Slow acetylators build up isoniazid → peripheral neuritis and hepatotoxicity.

bank.q: In slow acetylators, procainamide may cause...
bank.why: Acetylator phenotype: isoniazid → neuritis, hepatotoxicity; procainamide → lupus.

bank.q: Hydralazine, an oral vasodilator for hypertension, is metabolized by which Phase 2 reaction?
bank.why: Hydralazine and procainamide are acetylated by NATs, like isoniazid. (Links Lesson 2 to Lesson 6.)

bank.q: Which antihypertensive is listed among the methylated drugs?
bank.why: MT drugs: L-dopa, methyldopa, mercaptopurine, captopril (an ACE inhibitor, Lesson 6).

bank.q: COMT methylates norepinephrine into...
bank.why: COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) methylates catecholamines: NE → normetanephrine.

bank.q: Azathioprine becomes 6-mercaptopurine, which is cleared by TPMT and xanthine oxidase. What happens with low TPMT activity?
bank.a: 6-thioguanine nucleotides build up to toxic levels
d: 6-Mercaptopurine is cleared faster and loses its effect
Xanthine oxidase stops working, so uric acid falls
Azathioprine is no longer converted to 6-mercaptopurine
bank.why: Low TPMT (methylation) → less clearance of 6-MP → toxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides.

bank.q: About 90% of a normal acetaminophen dose is metabolized by...
bank.why: ~90% → glucuronide and sulfate (safe); ~5–9% → CYP2E1 → NAPQI.

bank.q: Which enzyme turns acetaminophen into its toxic metabolite NAPQI?
bank.why: CYP2E1 makes NAPQI, the one ethanol induces.

bank.q: What normally neutralizes NAPQI?
bank.why: Glutathione binds NAPQI; when it runs out in an overdose, NAPQI kills hepatocytes.

bank.q: A heavy drinker takes extra acetaminophen for a hangover and develops liver failure. Why is he at higher risk?
bank.a: Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1, so more NAPQI is made
d: Alcohol inhibits UGT, so more acetaminophen is glucuronidated
bank.why: Ethanol is a potent CYP2E1 inducer; more acetaminophen goes down the NAPQI pathway.

bank.q: N-acetylcysteine helps in acetaminophen overdose by...
bank.why: NAC refills glutathione to neutralize NAPQI.

bank.q: Phase 2 conjugation makes a drug much more water-soluble.
bank.why: Phase 2 attaches a large polar group, so the metabolite is easily excreted.

bank.q: Most of a normal dose of acetaminophen goes to NAPQI through CYP2E1.
bank.why: Only about 5–9% goes through CYP2E1; about 90% is glucuronidated or sulfated.

bank.q: The three functions of the nervous system are...
bank.a: Sensory input, integration and motor output
bank.why: Sensory input → integration → motor output.

bank.q: Which division of the ANS arises from the thoracolumbar spinal cord (T1–L2)?
bank.why: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar; parasympathetic = craniosacral.

bank.q: The parasympathetic nervous system comes from which roots?
bank.why: Parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem cranial nerves and S2–S4). This was a past quiz item.

bank.q: Which describes the parasympathetic division?
bank.a: Long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers; ganglia near the organ
d: Short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibers; ganglia near the spinal cord
Only one neuron from the CNS to the organ
bank.why: Parasympathetic: long pre, short post, ganglia at the organ. Sympathetic: short pre, long post, ganglia near the cord.
bank.hint: Its ganglia sit at the organ.

bank.q: All preganglionic autonomic fibers release...
bank.why: All preganglionic fibers (both divisions) release ACh onto nicotinic Nn receptors.

bank.q: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release...
bank.why: Sympathetic postganglionic → NE on adrenergic receptors (except sweat glands, which get ACh).

bank.q: Which organ receives sympathetic postganglionic fibers that release acetylcholine?
bank.why: Eccrine sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic (muscarinic).

bank.q: The adrenal medulla releases mainly ___ into the blood.
bank.why: The adrenal medulla (a modified sympathetic ganglion) releases epinephrine (and some NE).

bank.q: At the skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction, ACh acts on...
bank.why: Somatic NMJ → ACh on Nm (nicotinic muscle). Nn = ganglia, CNS.

bank.q: Which statement does NOT describe the sympathetic nervous system?
bank.a: Its postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine as a rule
d: It arises from the thoracolumbar cord
Its preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors
bank.why: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons release NE (except to sweat glands). Past quiz item.

bank.q: Which is NOT a sympathetic response?
bank.why: Fight or flight slows the gut (decreased peristalsis) and contracts sphincters, dilates pupils and makes you sweat. More peristalsis is parasympathetic.
bank.hint: Rest and digest moves the gut.

bank.q: Which finding is NOT part of the anticholinergic toxidrome?
bank.why: Anticholinergic: hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat (mydriasis), mad as a hatter. Miosis is cholinergic.
bank.hint: Blind as a bat = big pupils.

bank.q: Which is NOT seen in cholinergic (organophosphate) toxicity?
bank.why: DUMBBELLS: Diarrhea/diaphoresis, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm/bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lethargy, Lacrimation, Salivation. Pupils are small, not dilated.

bank.q: In DUMBBELLS (cholinergic toxicity), the M stands for...
bank.why: Excess ACh constricts the pupil (miosis).

bank.q: A farmer who sprayed pesticide has pinpoint pupils, drooling, sweating, diarrhea and a slow heart rate. Which toxidrome is this?
bank.why: Wet + slow + small pupils = cholinergic (organophosphates inhibit AChE).

bank.q: A child is hot, dry, flushed, has dilated pupils, a fast heart rate and is confused. Which toxidrome?
bank.why: Hot, dry, red, blind (mydriasis), mad = anticholinergic.

bank.q: In the anticholinergic toxidrome, "blind as a bat" refers to...
d: Miosis and spasm of accommodation (pinpoint pupils)
Night blindness from vitamin A deficiency
Retinal bleeding from a sudden rise in BP
bank.why: Blocking M3 in the eye dilates the pupil and paralyzes accommodation.

bank.q: Hyperthermia is a feature of which toxidrome?
bank.why: No sweating (blocked muscarinic sweat glands) → hot as a hare. Cholinergic poisoning causes sweating instead. Past quiz: hyperthermia is NOT seen in cholinergic toxicity.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the uptake of choline into the cholinergic nerve terminal?
bank.why: He Vests Botox, then Stops: hemicholinium (choline uptake), vesamicol (storage), botulinum (release), -stigmines (AChE).

bank.q: Which drug blocks the storage of acetylcholine in vesicles?
bank.why: Vesamicol blocks the vesicular ACh transporter (VAT). Reserpine is the look-alike for catecholamines (blocks VMAT). Past quiz item.
bank.hint: Not reserpine: that one is for catecholamines.

bank.q: Botulinum toxin blocks...
bank.a: Release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal
d: Synthesis of ACh by choline acetyltransferase
Binding of ACh to nicotinic receptors
bank.why: Botulinum cleaves the SNARE proteins needed for vesicle fusion, so ACh isn't released. Past quiz item.

bank.q: After eating home-canned food, a patient develops descending flaccid paralysis. The toxin acts on...
bank.a: SNARE proteins needed to release ACh
bank.why: Botulinum toxin destroys SNAREs → no ACh release → flaccid paralysis.

bank.q: Acetylcholine is made from acetyl-CoA and choline by...
bank.why: ChAT synthesizes ACh; AChE breaks it down.
bank.hint: It transfers an acetyl to choline.

bank.q: Acetylcholinesterase breaks ACh into...
bank.why: AChE hydrolyzes ACh → choline + acetate; choline is taken back up.

bank.q: Which drugs block the termination step (acetylcholinesterase)?
d: Vesamicol, which blocks ACh storage in vesicles
Botulinum toxin, which blocks ACh release
bank.why: AChE inhibitors (carbamates, organophosphates) are the indirect-acting cholinomimetics.

bank.q: Which muscarinic receptor slows the heart?
bank.why: M2 = heart (↓cAMP, opens K+ channels). M1 = nerves, M3 = glands and smooth muscle, M4/M5 = CNS.

bank.q: Which muscarinic receptor mediates gland secretion and smooth muscle contraction?
bank.why: M3 = glands and smooth muscle (IP3/DAG): saliva, tears, sweat, bladder, bronchi.

bank.q: M1 receptors are found mainly on...
bank.why: M1 = nerves (IP3/DAG); M1 blockers (pirenzepine) reduce gastric acid.
bank.hint: M2 is the heart; M3 is glands and smooth muscle.

bank.q: M2 activation slows the heart by...
bank.a: Decreasing cAMP and opening K+ channels
d: Increasing IP3 and DAG and releasing Ca2+
Opening Na+ channels and depolarizing the SA node
Increasing cAMP and closing K+ channels
bank.why: M2 is Gi-coupled: less cAMP and more K+ outflow → slower firing.

bank.q: Nicotinic receptors are...
bank.why: Nicotinic = ion channels (Na+/K+); muscarinic = G-protein receptors.

bank.q: Nn receptors are found in...
bank.why: Nn = neurons (ganglia, CNS); Nm = muscle.

bank.q: Muscarinic receptors are G protein-coupled receptors.
bank.why: M1–M5 are G-protein receptors; nicotinic receptors are ion channels.

bank.q: A day after delivery, Mrs. Garcia cannot urinate, and there is no obstruction. Which drug helps her bladder empty?
bank.why: Bethanechol (choline ester) contracts the bladder: for nonobstructive urinary and bowel retention. Methacholine = asthma challenge, pilocarpine = dry mouth, oxybutynin = the opposite (blocks M3 for incontinence).
bank.hint: A choline ester that acts on the bladder, not the one used for asthma testing.

bank.q: Which drug is inhaled to provoke bronchoconstriction when diagnosing asthma?
bank.why: Methacholine challenge test: people with asthma bronchoconstrict at low doses. Ipratropium and salbutamol are bronchodilators.

bank.q: A woman with Sjögren syndrome complains of a very dry mouth and dry eyes. Which drug increases her saliva and tears?
bank.why: Pilocarpine (alkaloid, M3-selective) stimulates lacrimal and salivary glands: used for Sjögren and sicca syndrome. Atropine and scopolamine would dry her more.

bank.q: What is the most common side effect of pilocarpine?
bank.why: Pilocarpine stimulates all M3 glands, sweat glands included.

bank.q: Pilocarpine is an alkaloid that acts selectively on...
bank.why: Pilocarpine = muscarinic alkaloid, selective for M3 (glands).

bank.q: Acetylcholine itself is used clinically as...
bank.why: ACh constricts the pupil (miosis); it is used as a miotic in the eye.

bank.q: Which drug activates both Nn and Nm receptors (and all muscarinic receptors)?
bank.why: ACh, the natural transmitter, activates every cholinergic receptor. The choline esters and pilocarpine are muscarinic. Past quiz item.

bank.q: Which pair are choline esters?
bank.why: Choline esters (nonselective M1–M3): bethanechol, methacholine. Pilocarpine is an alkaloid; atropine and scopolamine block; neostigmine and edrophonium inhibit AChE.

bank.q: Toxicity from a muscarinic agonist is treated with...
bank.why: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors. The others would add more cholinergic effect.

bank.q: Mang Romy wants to quit smoking. Which partial nicotinic agonist helps?
bank.why: Varenicline (partial) and nicotine (full) are nicotinic agonists for smoking cessation. Succinylcholine = depolarizing NMJ blocker; hexamethonium = ganglion blocker; pancuronium = NMJ blocker.

bank.q: Smoking-cessation drugs such as nicotine and varenicline act on...
bank.why: They are nicotinic agonists; the past quiz key was "Nm and Nn receptors".

bank.q: Which neuromuscular blocker works by depolarizing the muscle membrane?
bank.why: Succinylcholine (suxamethonium) is an Nm agonist that depolarizes then paralyzes. The -curonium/-curium drugs are nondepolarizing curares (Lesson 4).

bank.q: In phase I of a succinylcholine block, the muscle shows...
bank.why: Phase I: depolarization → transient fasciculations → flaccid paralysis. Phase II: repolarized but desensitized.

bank.q: In phase II of a succinylcholine block...
bank.a: The membrane repolarizes but the receptor stays desensitized to ACh
d: The membrane stays depolarized and the channel stays open
The muscle fasciculates as the fibers depolarize again
ACh release from the nerve ending is blocked
bank.why: Phase II = repolarized but desensitized.

bank.q: Bethanechol acts mainly on muscarinic receptors.
bank.why: Bethanechol is a muscarinic choline ester; it was designed to avoid nicotinic effects and resist AChE.

bank.q: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics work by...
bank.why: They don't bind cholinoceptors; they make ACh last longer.

bank.q: A woman has drooping eyelids and weakness that worsen through the day. Which short-acting drug is used for the bedside diagnosis of myasthenia gravis?
bank.why: Edrophonium (Tensilon) is very short-acting: strength improves within minutes in myasthenia. Neostigmine treats it; physostigmine is for atropine overdose; malathion is a pesticide.

bank.q: The edrophonium test for myasthenia gravis is also called the...
bank.why: Tensilon is edrophonium's brand name; this was a VSA item.

bank.q: Which drug is used to TREAT myasthenia gravis long-term?
bank.why: Neostigmine and pyridostigmine (carbamates) treat myasthenia. Edrophonium is too short (diagnosis only); succinylcholine would cause paralysis.

bank.q: Which of these is a carbamate cholinesterase inhibitor?
bank.why: Carbamates = the -stigmines (neostigmine, pyridostigmine, physostigmine). Edrophonium is an alcohol; parathion and malathion are organophosphates.

bank.q: A child who swallowed eye drops containing atropine is delirious, hot and dry. Which AChE inhibitor reaches the brain and reverses it?
bank.why: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that enters the CNS; it treats atropine (anticholinergic) overdose.

bank.q: Which is an irreversible AChE inhibitor used as a pesticide?
bank.why: Organophosphates (-thion: parathion, malathion) inhibit AChE irreversibly. -THION = THE ONE you can't undo.

bank.q: Which of these was a war nerve gas (WWII)?
bank.why: Tabun, sarin and soman are nerve gases; parathion and malathion are pesticides. All are organophosphates.
bank.hint: The other three are two pesticides and a short-acting test drug.

bank.q: What do nerve agents such as sarin directly target?
bank.why: Organophosphate nerve agents bind AChE irreversibly, so ACh builds up. Past quiz item.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT used for Alzheimer disease?
bank.why: Alzheimer drugs: donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine ("Si Don Pepe, may dementia. Pa Gala Gala sa Riva"). The past quiz version had physostigmine as the answer.

bank.q: Lolo Ben has slowly worsening memory loss diagnosed as Alzheimer disease. Which drug is used?
bank.why: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are AChE inhibitors for Alzheimer (cholinergic neurons are deficient).

bank.q: Why are AChE inhibitors used in Alzheimer dementia?
bank.a: Cholinergic neurons are deficient in Alzheimer disease
d: They increase dopamine in the brain
bank.why: Slides: cholinergic neurons are deficient, so making ACh last longer helps.

bank.q: Which lists the AChE inhibitors from SHORTEST to LONGEST acting?
bank.why: Short: edrophonium; intermediate: carbamates (-stigmines); very long: organophosphates (-thion).

bank.q: Physostigmine enters the CNS, which is why it is used for atropine overdose.
bank.why: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine and crosses into the brain; neostigmine does not.

bank.q: Organophosphates such as parathion are reversible AChE inhibitors.
bank.why: Organophosphates inhibit AChE irreversibly.

bank.q: The three groups of cholinergic antagonists are...
bank.why: Antimuscarinic (atropine…), antinicotinic (ganglion and NMJ blockers) and cholinesterase regenerators (oximes like pralidoxime).

bank.q: Pralidoxime (2-PAM) belongs to which group?
bank.why: Oximes regenerate AChE after organophosphate poisoning.

bank.q: A farmer poisoned with organophosphate pesticide is drooling, wheezing, with pinpoint pupils. Which drug is the first choice?
bank.why: Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects of the excess ACh: first choice for organophosphate poisoning (with pralidoxime). The other three add cholinergic effect.

bank.q: A patient's heart rate is 38/min and he feels faint. Which drug raises the heart rate by blocking vagal (muscarinic) tone?
bank.why: Atropine is used for symptomatic bradycardia; propranolol, neostigmine and pilocarpine would slow the heart more.

bank.q: During general anesthesia, atropine is given to...
bank.a: Prevent bradycardia and reduce saliva and airway secretions
d: Relax skeletal muscle so the trachea can be intubated
Induce sleep and deepen the anesthetic
Prevent malignant hyperthermia from volatile agents
bank.why: Slides: with anesthesia for bradycardia, hypersalivation and airway secretions.

bank.term: Pupil dilation for an eye exam
bank.q: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupils for a retinal exam. Which eye drop?
bank.why: Tropicamide (like atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate) is an antimuscarinic mydriatic. Pilocarpine constricts the pupil; tiotropium is inhaled.

bank.q: Christopher has COPD. Which inhaled drug blocks bronchial muscarinic receptors and has the longest half-life?
bank.why: -tropium drugs (ipratropium, tiotropium) plus umeclidinium and glycopyrronium are inhaled for asthma and COPD; tiotropium lasts longest.

bank.q: Which inhaled antimuscarinic has the longest half-life?
bank.why: Slides: tiotropium has the longest half-life.

bank.q: Reine gets seasick on every boat trip. Which antimuscarinic prevents motion sickness?
bank.why: Scopolamine (a stereoisomer of atropine) crosses the blood-brain barrier better → motion sickness. Scop = sea.

bank.q: Why is scopolamine preferred over atropine for motion sickness?
bank.a: It crosses the blood-brain barrier better
d: It acts only on M2 receptors
bank.why: Scopolamine reaches the CNS better than atropine.

bank.q: Lola Ising leaks urine whenever she feels a sudden urge to void. Which drug relaxes the bladder?
bank.why: Oxybutynin (M3 blocker) for urge incontinence. Bethanechol does the opposite (retention); tamsulosin is for BPH; dicyclomine is the M3 blocker for diarrhea.

bank.q: Which M3 blocker is used for diarrhea?
bank.why: Dicyclomine (dicycloverine) for diarrhea; oxybutynin for the bladder; pirenzepine for ulcers.

bank.q: Which M1-selective blocker lowers gastric acid in peptic ulcer disease?
bank.why: Pirenzepine and telenzepine (M1) reduce acid secretion → peptic ulcer disease.

bank.q: Which drug blocks Nn receptors in the autonomic ganglia and was once used for hypertension?
bank.why: Hexamethonium is the ganglionic (Nn) blocker, now obsolete.

bank.q: Before surgery, an anesthesiologist gives a drug that blocks Nm receptors to relax skeletal muscle. Which drug did the anesthesiologist give?
bank.why: Curares (tubocurarine, pancuronium, atracurium, vecuronium) block Nm at the NMJ.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a neuromuscular (curare-like) blocker?
bank.why: Hexamethonium blocks ganglia (Nn), not the NMJ (Nm).

bank.q: Scopolamine is related to atropine as its...
bank.why: Slides: scopolamine is a stereoisomer of atropine.

bank.q: Atropine blocks all muscarinic receptors.
bank.why: Atropine is the nonselective prototype muscarinic blocker.

bank.q: Which is NOT a catecholamine?
bank.why: The catecholamines are norepinephrine, epinephrine and dopamine.

bank.q: What is the order of catecholamine synthesis?
bank.why: Tyrosine hydroxylase → AAAD → dopamine β-hydroxylase → PNMT.

bank.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis?
bank.why: Tyrosine hydroxylase (tyrosine → L-DOPA) is rate-limiting; metyrosine inhibits it.

bank.q: Which enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla?
bank.why: PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase) adds the methyl that makes epinephrine.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase?
bank.why: Met Reserve Guards at Coco's: metyrosine (synthesis), reserpine (storage), guanethidine (release), cocaine/TCA (reuptake).

bank.q: Which drug blocks VMAT, so catecholamines can't be stored in vesicles?
bank.why: Reserpine blocks VMAT. Vesamicol is the cholinergic look-alike (blocks VAT for ACh).

bank.q: Which drug blocks the release of norepinephrine?
bank.why: Guanethidine blocks release; amphetamine and tyramine cause release; cocaine blocks reuptake.

bank.q: Which drug CAUSES the release of norepinephrine?
bank.why: Release is activated by amphetamines, ephedrine and tyramine.

bank.q: Steve's blood test shows cocaine. How does cocaine increase norepinephrine in the synapse?
bank.a: It blocks NE reuptake through NET
bank.why: Cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants block the reuptake transporters (NET, DAT), so NE stays in the synapse. (A midterm case started with "Steve has cocaine in his blood".)

bank.q: Which drug class blocks NE reuptake like cocaine?
bank.why: Termination by reuptake (NET) is blocked by cocaine and TCAs.

bank.q: Tyramine, found in aged cheese and cured meats, acts by...
bank.why: Tyramine is an NE releaser (a migraine trigger).

bank.q: Which food is rich in tyramine?
bank.why: Aged foods: cheese, cured meats, beer, soy sauce, overripe fruit.

bank.q: Vesamicol is to ACh storage as ___ is to catecholamine storage.
bank.why: Side by side: storage = vesamicol (ACh) vs reserpine (NE).

bank.q: Botulinum toxin is to ACh release as ___ is to NE release.
bank.why: Release: botulinum (ACh) vs guanethidine (NE).

bank.q: Which receptor increases heart rate and contractility?
bank.why: β1 = one heart; β2 = two lungs; α1 = squeeze (vasoconstriction); α2 = slow down (presynaptic brake).

bank.q: Which receptor causes bronchodilation?
bank.why: β2 = two lungs.

bank.q: Which receptor causes vasoconstriction and sphincter contraction?
bank.why: α1 = contraction (squeeze).

bank.q: Which receptor acts as a presynaptic brake on norepinephrine release?
bank.why: α2 = relaxation and the presynaptic brake; that's why α2 agonists (clonidine, methyldopa) lower BP.

bank.q: A patient in septic shock has a BP of 70/40 despite fluids. Which drug is first line?
bank.why: Norepinephrine (α1 > β1) raises peripheral resistance: first line in septic shock.

bank.q: Minutes after a bee sting, a boy has hives, wheezing and a falling BP. Which drug should he be given first?
bank.why: Epinephrine (β1 = β2 > α) opens the airways (β2), supports the heart (β1) and vessels (α): drug of choice in anaphylaxis (EpiPen).

bank.q: Epinephrine's receptor profile is...
bank.why: Epi = "every"one; NE = "no" β2 (α1 > β1 >>> β2).

bank.q: Norepinephrine's receptor profile is...
bank.why: Norepinephrine has little β2 effect ("no β2").

bank.q: At LOW doses, dopamine mainly stimulates...
bank.why: Dopamine climbs D → β → α as the dose rises.

bank.q: At HIGH doses, dopamine mainly stimulates...
bank.why: Low D1, middle β1, high α1.

bank.q: Dopamine is first line in septic shock when there is also...
bank.why: Slides: dopamine, first line in septic shock with renal shutdown (its D1 effect dilates renal vessels).

bank.q: Janah has a stuffy nose from a cold. Which nasal spray shrinks the nasal vessels?
bank.why: α1 agonists (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline) are decongestants.

bank.q: Which drug is an α1 agonist used as a decongestant?
bank.why: α1 agonists: phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline.

bank.q: Which α2 agonist is used for hypertension and off-label for ADHD and Tourette syndrome?
bank.why: Clonidine: α2 → hypertension; off-label ADHD and Tourette. Methyldopa is the α2 agonist for pregnancy.

bank.q: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks has preeclampsia. Which α2 agonist is used for her blood pressure?
bank.why: Methyldopa = Mom's drug: gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.

bank.q: Which β1 agonist is used for cardiogenic shock and cardiac stress testing?
bank.why: Dobutamine (β1) DOBUles the heart's pumping.

bank.q: A student with asthma has an acute attack with wheezing. Which drug relieves the bronchospasm?
bank.why: Salbutamol (albuterol) is a β2 agonist (two lungs). Propranolol would make it worse.

bank.q: A woman at 30 weeks is in preterm labor. Which β2 agonist relaxes the uterus (tocolysis)?
bank.why: β2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline, isoxsuprine) relax smooth muscle of the lungs and uterus.

bank.q: Common side effects of salbutamol are...
bank.why: β2 agonists: tachycardia, tremors, nervousness, restlessness.

bank.q: Isoproterenol is a...
d: Mixed α and β blocker (like labetalol)
bank.why: Isoproterenol acts on all β receptors; used for asthma.

bank.q: Norepinephrine is a strong β2 agonist.
bank.why: Norepinephrine: α1 > β1 >>> β2. It has very little β2 effect.

bank.q: A woman with episodes of palpitations, headache and excessive sweating has a pheochromocytoma. Which drug is given before surgery?
bank.why: PHEochromocytoma → PHEnoxybenzamine or PHEntolamine (nonselective α blockers). Pheo triad: palpitations, headache, excessive sweating.

bank.q: Which α blocker binds irreversibly?
bank.why: Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible; phentolamine = reversible. Both nonselective.

bank.q: Which nonselective α blocker is reversible?
bank.why: Phentolamine = reversible nonselective α blocker.

bank.q: Mang Lito, 65, has a weak urine stream from an enlarged prostate. Which drug relaxes the prostate and is the most prostate-selective?
bank.why: α1 blockers (-zosin: prazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin) treat BPH; tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective. Pee-zosin.

bank.q: After his first dose of a new pill for BPH, Mr. Aquino nearly faints when he stands up. Which drug most likely caused it?
bank.why: α1 blockers cause orthostatic hypotension (vessels can't constrict on standing).

bank.q: Yohimbine is a(n)...
bank.why: Yohimbine blocks α2; obsolete; was used for orthostatic hypotension and erectile dysfunction.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is cardioselective (β1)?
bank.why: β1-selective = MANBABE: metoprolol, atenolol, nebivolol, bisoprolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol. Propranolol, timolol and pindolol are nonselective.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is NONselective?
bank.why: LOL trick: A–N = β1-selective; O–Z = nonselective (propranolol, timolol).
bank.hint: Starts with a letter after N.

bank.q: Which drug blocks both α and β receptors?
bank.why: Names ending in -lol but not -olol (labetalol, carvedilol) block α and β.

bank.q: Using the "LOL" trick, labetalol is...
bank.why: -lol but not -olol = α and β.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is the shortest-acting and given IV?
bank.why: Esmolol: shortest-acting, IV (in MANBABE).

bank.q: Which β-blocker is used to prevent migraine?
bank.why: Slides: propranolol for migraine prophylaxis (also hyperthyroidism).

bank.q: A hypertensive patient also has asthma. If a β-blocker must be used, which is the safer choice?
bank.why: Cardioselective (β1) blockers spare the β2 receptors in the lungs. Propranolol, timolol and pindolol block β2 and can trigger bronchospasm.

bank.q: Which is NOT a β1-selective blocker (not in MANBABE)?
bank.why: MANBABE: metoprolol, atenolol, nebivolol, bisoprolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol.

bank.q: A woman with hyperthyroidism has palpitations and tremors. Which drug controls these symptoms?
bank.why: Slides: β-blockers are used in hyperthyroidism (and post-MI, hypertension, heart failure).

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed use of β-blockers?
bank.why: Uses: post-MI, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, migraine. β-blockers can worsen asthma.

bank.q: Tamsulosin is the α1 blocker most selective for the prostate.
bank.why: Slides: tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective -zosin.

bank.q: Atenolol is a nonselective β-blocker.
bank.why: Atenolol starts with A (A–N), so it's β1-selective (the A in MANBABE).

bank.q: Endocrine glands secrete their products...
bank.a: Directly into the blood as hormones
bank.why: Exocrine glands use ducts; endocrine glands release hormones into the blood.

bank.q: A hormone that acts on NEARBY cells is acting in a ___ manner.
bank.why: Circulating (endocrine) = far; paracrine = nearby cells; autocrine = the same cell.

bank.q: Lipid-soluble hormones such as steroids and thyroid hormone act by...
bank.a: Entering the cell and binding a nuclear receptor to make new proteins
d: Binding a surface receptor and starting a second-messenger cascade
Staying in the blood without entering cells
bank.why: Lipid-soluble hormones cross the membrane → nuclear receptor → gene transcription. Water-soluble (amines, peptides) use surface receptors.

bank.q: In the thyroid axis, T3 and T4 inhibit TRH and TSH release. This is an example of...
bank.why: Hypothalamus TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4, which shuts down both.
bank.hint: The product turns off its own signal.

bank.q: About 99% of the pancreas consists of...
bank.why: The pancreas is both exocrine (99% acini) and endocrine (islets scattered among the acini).

bank.q: Pancreatic alpha (A) cells secrete...
bank.why: Alpha (17%) = glucagon; beta (70%) = insulin; delta (7%) = somatostatin; F = pancreatic polypeptide.

bank.q: Which islet cells make insulin and are the largest share (about 70%)?
bank.why: Beta = biggest share, makes insulin.

bank.q: Delta (D) cells secrete...
bank.why: Delta (7%) = somatostatin.
bank.hint: The hormone that holds back both insulin and glucagon.

bank.q: F cells of the islets secrete...
bank.why: F cells = pancreatic polypeptide.

bank.q: Which is the hormone of the fasting state?
bank.why: Glucagon raises glucose during fasting by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

bank.q: Which of these is a counterregulatory hormone (opposes insulin)?
bank.why: Counterregulatory: glucagon, growth hormone, cortisol, epinephrine (stress and fasting hormones).

bank.q: Insulin consists of...
bank.a: An A chain and a B chain joined by disulfide bridges
d: A single peptide chain with no disulfide bridges
A steroid ring made from cholesterol
bank.why: Proinsulin = A chain + B chain + C-peptide; the C-peptide is cut out.

bank.q: A patient may be secretly injecting insulin. Which lab marker shows whether high insulin comes from her own pancreas?
bank.why: C-peptide is cut from proinsulin, so it accompanies the body's own insulin; injected insulin has none. (Midterm true-or-false: C-peptide differentiates endogenous from exogenous insulin = True.)
bank.hint: The piece cut out of proinsulin.

bank.q: After glucose enters the β-cell through GLUT2 and ATP rises, what happens next?
bank.a: The ATP-sensitive K+ channel closes → depolarization → Ca2+ enters → insulin exocytosis
d: The K+ channel opens → hyperpolarization → insulin release stops
Ca2+ leaves the cell → insulin is released
Glucagon is released first, then insulin
bank.why: Sulfonylureas act on this same K+ channel to force insulin release.

bank.q: Insulin makes muscle and fat take up glucose by moving which transporter to the cell membrane?
bank.why: GLUT-2 is the β-cell sensor; GLUT-4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and fat.

bank.q: In the liver, insulin...
d: Increases ketone production from fatty acids
bank.why: Insulin stores fuel: ↑ glycogen and fat synthesis, ↓ glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

bank.q: In adipose tissue, insulin...
bank.a: Increases triglyceride storage and decreases lipolysis
d: Increases lipolysis and fatty acid release
Increases ketone release into the blood
bank.why: Insulin stores fat.

bank.q: The classic "3 Ps" of diabetes are...
bank.why: Appetite, thirst and urination.

bank.q: Which is typical of type 1 diabetes?
bank.a: Autoimmune β-cell destruction; ketoacidosis is common
d: Insulin resistance in an obese adult
Treated first with diet, exercise and oral drugs
bank.why: Type 1: autoimmune, absolute insulin deficiency, usually < 30 years, thin, sudden, ketoacidosis common, 50% twin concordance.

bank.q: Which is typical of type 2 diabetes?
bank.a: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
d: Insulin dependence from the very start
bank.why: Type 2: insulin resistance + relative deficiency, adults, often obese, ketoacidosis rare, 90% twin concordance. Type 2 is 90–95% of all diabetes.

bank.q: The twin concordance of type 2 diabetes is about...
bank.why: Type 1 ~50%, type 2 ~90% (stronger genetics).

bank.q: Which is a risk of gestational diabetes?
d: Lower risk of later type 2 diabetes
bank.why: Gestational DM risks: pre-eclampsia, macrosomia, cesarean delivery and later type 2 DM.

bank.q: Justyn: waist 105 cm, triglycerides 160 mg/dL, HDL 45 mg/dL, BP 128/82, fasting glucose 98 mg/dL. Does he have metabolic syndrome?
bank.a: No, only 2 of the 5 criteria are met
bank.why: Criteria (3 of 5 needed): waist ≥102 cm in men ✓; TG ≥150 ✓; HDL <40 in men ✗ (45); BP ≥130/85 ✗; fasting glucose ≥100 ✗. Only 2.

bank.q: Which patient meets the criteria for diabetes?
d: Josh: thirsty and urinating often, random glucose 199 mg/dL
bank.why: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% is diagnostic. A random glucose must be ≥200 with symptoms (199 is not), fasting must be ≥126. This mirrors the midterm item.

bank.q: A fasting plasma glucose diagnostic of diabetes is...
bank.why: Fasting ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mM). ≥100 is a metabolic syndrome criterion.

bank.q: A random plasma glucose diagnostic of diabetes (with symptoms) is...
bank.why: Random ≥200 with symptoms, or 2-h OGTT ≥200.

bank.q: An HbA1c diagnostic of diabetes is...
bank.why: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% diagnoses diabetes; the treatment target is < 7%.

bank.q: HbA1c reflects blood glucose control over the past...
bank.why: HbA1c follows the ~120-day lifespan of red blood cells.

bank.q: What is the usual HbA1c target in diabetes management?
bank.why: Glycemic targets: HbA1c < 7%, relaxed to < 8% in the frail elderly.

bank.q: The pre-meal glucose target is...
bank.why: Pre-meal 90–130 mg/dL (5–7.2 mmol/L); 1-h postprandial < 180; 2-h postprandial < 150.

bank.q: The 2-hour postprandial glucose target is...
bank.why: 1-h postprandial < 180; 2-h postprandial < 150.

bank.q: The blood pressure target for diabetic patients in the lesson is...
bank.why: BP < 140/90 (the same number that starts treatment in the hypertension algorithm, Lesson 6).

bank.q: A 60-kg patient with type 1 diabetes starts insulin. Using the lesson's rule, about how many units per day?
bank.why: Insulin units per day ≈ weight (kg) × 0.55 = 60 × 0.55 = 33.

bank.q: What comes first in treating type 2 diabetes?
bank.a: Caloric restriction and more exercise, then metformin
bank.why: Type 2: lifestyle first, then metformin; add oral agents or insulin based on HbA1c.

bank.q: Which fats are recommended in the diabetic diet?
d: Saturated animal fats (butter, lard, fatty meat)
Coconut and palm oils used for frying
bank.why: Mediterranean-style diet with monounsaturated fats.

bank.q: Which is a MACROvascular complication of diabetes?
bank.why: Micro = eyes, kidneys, nerves; macro = brain (stroke), heart (MI), legs (peripheral vascular disease).

bank.q: Which findings are signs of diabetic retinopathy?
d: Cataract and glaucoma, with no retinal changes
Blue sclera and a cherry-red spot
bank.why: Retinopathy: aneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots.

bank.q: Where are incretins (GLP-1, GIP) made?
bank.why: Incretins are gut hormones released after an oral glucose load; they boost insulin and block glucagon. (Midterm item.)

bank.q: C-peptide can tell the body's own insulin from injected insulin.
bank.why: C-peptide is released with endogenous insulin; injected insulin contains none. (Midterm item.)

bank.q: Which insulin is RAPID-acting?
bank.why: Rapid = LAG: lispro, aspart, glulisine (onset 5–15 min). Glargine = long, NPH = intermediate, regular = short.

bank.q: Which insulin is given IV in emergencies such as diabetic ketoacidosis?
bank.why: Regular is the only one that goes Right into the vein.
bank.hint: R for right into the vein.

bank.q: Which insulin lasts the longest (> 42 hours)?
bank.why: Long = GDD: glargine ~24 h, detemir 17 h, degludec > 42 h (De-gludec lasts De-cades).

bank.q: Which insulin has a flat profile with no peak?
bank.why: Long-acting analogs (glargine, detemir, degludec) are flat; NPH peaks at 6–7 h.

bank.q: NPH insulin is...
bank.why: NPH (neutral protamine Hagedorn): onset 2–4 h, peak 6–7 h, lasts 10–20 h.

bank.q: An insulin with onset 5–15 minutes, peak 1–1.5 hours, lasting 3–4 hours is...
bank.why: Those are the rapid-acting numbers; taken with meals.

bank.q: What is the most common side effect of insulin?
bank.why: Hypoglycemia: shaking, fast heart rate, hunger, sweating, confusion, dizziness.

bank.q: Which is NOT a sign of hypoglycemia?
bank.why: Hypoglycemia: shaking, fast heart rate, hunger, sweating, confusion, dizziness. Polyuria is a sign of HIGH glucose.

bank.q: Which insulin combination mimics normal secretion in type 1 diabetes?
bank.a: Glargine once a day plus lispro with meals
d: NPH alone, once a day in the morning
Glipizide plus metformin, with no insulin
bank.why: Type 1: 3–4 injections a day; rapid + long-acting analogs (basal + mealtime). Glargine is the long-acting (basal) analog; lispro is the rapid-acting one taken with meals.

bank.q: Detemir is a ___ insulin lasting about 17 hours.
bank.why: GDD: glargine, detemir, degludec are long-acting.

bank.q: Regular insulin is the insulin used IV in emergencies.
bank.why: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the one given IV.

bank.q: Which drug increases insulin release from the β-cells of the pancreas?
bank.why: Tolbutamide is a 1st-generation sulfonylurea: it closes the β-cell K+ channel to release insulin. Metformin (biguanide) lowers liver glucose output, miglitol (α-glucosidase inhibitor) slows carb digestion, pioglitazone (TZD) sensitizes tissues. Dr. Orig read this one out after the midterm.

bank.q: Kyle, a 60-year-old hypertensive and diabetic, was found confused and wandering around the house. She was also sweating and trembling. Which drug does she most likely take?
bank.why: Confusion + sweating + trembling = hypoglycemia. Glipizide (2nd-gen sulfonylurea) forces insulin release even when glucose is low. Exenatide (GLP-1 agonist) and sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) work only when glucose is high; rosiglitazone (TZD) is a sensitizer. Dr. Orig's own example from the midterm.
bank.hint: First name the problem (hypo- or hyperglycemia), then the class.

bank.q: Which drug is MOST likely to cause hypoglycemia when used alone?
bank.why: Sulfonylureas (glimepiride) cause hypoglycemia; metformin, acarbose and DPP-4 inhibitors rarely do on their own.
bank.hint: The one that squeezes the β-cell.

bank.q: Theresa takes a pill just before each meal; it works like a sulfonylurea but faster and shorter, to control post-meal glucose. Which drug is Theresa taking?
bank.why: Meglitinides (-glinide: repaglinide, mitiglinide) hit the same K+ channel as sulfonylureas with a faster onset and shorter action.

bank.q: Sulfonylureas increase insulin release by...
bank.a: Closing the ATP-sensitive K+ channel of the β-cell
d: Activating AMPK in the liver (like metformin)
Binding PPAR-gamma in fat and muscle
Inhibiting DPP-4, so incretins last longer
bank.why: They block K+ efflux → depolarization → Ca2+ in → insulin out.

bank.q: Which is a FIRST-generation sulfonylurea?
bank.why: 1st gen (no longer used): tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, tolazamide. 2nd gen (more potent): glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride, gliclazide.

bank.q: Which is a SECOND-generation sulfonylurea?
bank.why: 2nd gen starts with gli- and ends in -ide.

bank.q: The major side effect of gliclazide is...
bank.why: Sulfonylureas: hypoglycemia (gliclazide is the slide's example) and weight gain.

bank.q: Glyburide belongs to which class?
bank.why: gli-…-ide = sulfonylurea.

bank.q: Mitiglinide belongs to which class?
bank.why: -glinide = meglitinide.

bank.q: Which drug activates AMPK to reduce glucose production by the liver?
bank.why: Metformin (biguanide) activates AMPK → ↓ hepatic glucose output.

bank.q: Which drug is first line for type 2 diabetes?
bank.why: Lifestyle, then metformin first.

bank.q: A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and insulin resistance is started on an antidiabetic drug. Which one?
bank.why: Metformin is also used in PCOS.

bank.q: After years of diabetes treatment, Gian has numb feet and low vitamin B12. Which drug is the likely cause?
bank.why: Metformin SEs = GLB: GI upset, lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency.

bank.q: A diabetic patient with kidney failure develops lactic acidosis. Which drug is most likely responsible?
bank.why: Lactic acidosis is the L in metformin's GLB.

bank.q: What is the most common side effect of metformin?
bank.why: GI effects are the most common; metformin alone doesn't cause hypoglycemia and is weight-neutral or causes loss.

bank.q: Which drug is a PPAR-gamma ligand that makes tissues respond better to insulin?
bank.why: Thiazolidinediones (-glitazone: pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) bind the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma.

bank.q: A diabetic with heart failure gets worse leg swelling and breathlessness after a new antidiabetic drug. Which drug was most likely started?
bank.why: TZD SEs = FAB-W: fluid retention/heart failure, anemia, bone fractures, weight gain.

bank.q: A postmenopausal diabetic woman has a wrist fracture after a minor fall. Which of her drugs adds to bone loss?
bank.why: TZDs cause bone loss (fractures): the B in FAB-W.

bank.q: An obese diabetic wants a weekly injection that lowers glucose and body weight by acting like a gut hormone. Which drug fits?
bank.why: GLP-1 agonists (-glutide, exenatide) mimic the incretin GLP-1: more insulin, less glucagon, and weight loss.

bank.q: Weeks after starting an injectable antidiabetic, a patient has severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. Which drug is linked to acute pancreatitis?
bank.why: GLP-1 agonists: GI disturbances and acute pancreatitis.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits the enzyme that breaks down incretins?
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin) keep the body's own incretins active. Exenatide is the GLP-1 agonist (look-alike trap).

bank.q: Since starting a new oral antidiabetic, Harly has had a stuffy, sore nose and throat and headaches. Which drug is Harly most likely taking?
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors: headache, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection.

bank.q: Which antidiabetic is weight NEUTRAL?
bank.why: Weight neutral: DPP-4 inhibitors and α-glucosidase inhibitors.
